name: Iranian Languages

formality.description: Iranian languages typically have elaborate politeness systems. Persian (Farsi) has an extremely rich taarof system with multiple levels of formality affecting pronouns (to/shomā), verb conjugation, vocabulary (separate 'eat' verbs for formal/informal), and elaborate self-deprecating/other-elevating conventions. Kurdish and other Iranian languages have simpler but still significant T-V systems.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Most modern Iranian languages have lost grammatical gender. Persian, Tajik, and Kurdish (Sorani) have no grammatical gender — third-person pronouns are gender-neutral (Persian u/ān). Kurdish (Kurmanji) is an exception that retains masculine/feminine gender. Some Pamir languages also retain gender. When translating from gendered source languages, gender is typically expressed lexically.

linguisticChallenges.ezafeConstruction: Iranian languages use the ezāfe (ezafe) construction to link nouns to their modifiers — a connecting particle (Persian -e/-ye, Kurdish -î/-y) between the head noun and its adjective, possessor, or complement. The chain can extend to multiple modifiers: ketāb-e bozorg-e sabz-e man 'my big green book'. This left-branching modifier structure is the reverse of English word order.
linguisticChallenges.lightVerbSystem: Persian and other Iranian languages form the vast majority of their predicates using light verb constructions — a noun, adjective, or preverb combined with a small set of light verbs (kardan 'do', shodan 'become', zadan 'hit', dādan 'give', etc.). There are hundreds of these combinations, and they cannot be predicted from their components: gush dādan 'ear give' = 'to listen'.
linguisticChallenges.complexPredicates: Beyond light verbs, Iranian languages use complex predicates with preverbs that modify verb meaning. The preverb system creates extensive polysemy and idiomatic expressions that require memorization rather than compositional analysis.
linguisticChallenges.splitErgativity: Some Iranian languages (Kurdish Kurmanji, Pashto, and some others) show split ergativity — ergative-absolutive alignment in past tenses but nominative-accusative in present tenses. This means the same verb has different argument-marking patterns in different tenses.
linguisticChallenges.scriptVariation: Iranian languages are split between Arabic-derived scripts (Persian, Pashto, Kurdish Sorani — written RTL) and Latin script (Kurdish Kurmanji, Tajik historically). Tajik uses Cyrillic. This script split within a single genus requires handling multiple directionalities.
linguisticChallenges.differentialObjectMarking: Persian uses the postposition -rā to mark specific/definite direct objects, while indefinite objects are unmarked. This differential object marking has no exact English equivalent — translating 'a book' vs. 'the book' requires choosing whether to use -rā.

notes: Genus card for Iranian languages (Persian/Farsi, Dari, Tajik, Kurdish, Pashto, Balochi, Ossetian, etc.). Script is null because members use Arabic-derived scripts (RTL), Latin, and Cyrillic. Direction is null because of the RTL/LTR split. Gender is marked false since most major members have lost it (Kurmanji being a notable exception).

regions.region: Iran, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Kurdistan (Iraq/Turkey/Syria), Pakistan (Pashto/Balochi), Caucasus (Ossetian)
